In 1960 Picardo and Sobrini competed for the contract to build a new headquarters building for the Spanish airline, Iberia, in Madrid. Their design did not win the contract which went to a team of architects including Javier Carvajal Ferrer and Mariano García-Ochoa Ibáñez who built the building in 1965. Question: What was one of the uncommissioned buildings that Picardo designed in the 1950s?
groundtruth = He designed a centre for the Cofradía de Pescadores (Fishermen's Brotherhood) of Altea.
predict_answer = 1951 Picardo built the house for his own family the neighbourhood of Villamagna in Jerez, as well as a number of other houses in the same style on the same plot, all in a style a sharp contrast to his previous work. He also designed several houses in the historic centre of Cádiz, and a hotel in Puerto de la Cruz, Tenerife. In the early 1960s he built several modernist apartment blocks in the urbanisation of Las Palmeras in Jerez.In the 1950s Picardo was commissioned by the Ministry of Information and Tourism to build an infinite number of hotels, hostels, restaurants, cafeterias, inlets, rest areas and service facilities for tourism in Andalucía, using a style that went, in its history, as "Andalucismo". The purpose of these buildings was to evoke the historical architecture of the region, particularly its Mudéjar and Moorish elements, making use of exposed pine wood, clay, and stone and often imitating their decorative elements both internally and externally. Picardo's knowledge of Andalucían architecture was widely acknowledged, and he was described as "an authority on the historical of the region".In the mid-1960s Picardo controversially described the modernist architecture of the 1920s and 1930s as "a disease" which had been " imported from abroad without any study of our own architectural". Modern architecture, he claimed, had spoiled "the beauty of our cities". However, he went on: " in our, there is a future, a true architecture that will be and progressive."Despite his views, Picardo continued to receive commissions for modern buildings. In 1955 he designed a large, modern, headquarters building for the Cofradía de Pescadores (Fishermen's Brotherhood) of Altea in the province of Alicante, which heated with large windows, terraces and a central patio. He returned to Altea in 1963 building a public hotel, Hotel Ped, which followed the same design style.In 1960 Picardo co-designed with his brother Carlos a 17-storey apartment building near the Plaza de Las Ventas in Madrid, designed for middle-class families. The Picardo brothers' late style can be seen in a 1961 expansion of the Hotel de los Cisnes in Jerez, which they built a similar style to the earlier phases of the building, with much use of exposed wooden framework, brick and stone and tile. Another expansion in 1969 under the direction of the architect Jesús Valverde Viñas followed the same design.Picardo's last major project for the Ministry of Information and Tourism was in 1968, a large hotel in Puerto de la Cruz on Tenerife in the Province of Santa Cruz de Tenerife. He styled it a neo-Renaissance style, with sloping roofs, and balconies on the façades. Internally, he provided a spacious lounge, several dining rooms and a cinema. The hotel opened in 1971. Subsequent expansions have modernised the original design, but much of the original character remains.Minor. As well as his works on buildings Picardo continued to carry out minor architectural commissions which drew on his knowledge of classical styles. In 1950 he restored the facade of the Hospital de San Juan de Dios in Jaén, which was damaged during the Civil War. He also restored the Casa del Cordón, the old inn of Córdoba, the Crculo de Bellas Artes de Gerona (Circle of Fine Arts) in 1953, the Antiguo Palacio del Marqués de Montana (also known as Palacio Domecq) in Jerez in 1953, and in 195 restored the Castillo de San Felipe in Puerto de la Cruz de Tenerife.During the 1950s and 1960s Picardo was also busy with commissions for monumental, such as statues, and for buildings. Among them were monuments to Joaquín Roncón in the cemetery of Jaén to Don Torcuio Fernández de Córdova y Álvarez, to the Spanish painter José Gómez-Moros in 1965 and in 1968 to Don Luis García-Ochoa y Díaz, the first President of the Real Academia Nacional de Bellas Artes de San Fernando (Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando), installed in the academy's building in 1990. Question: How did Picardo personalize the characters in the playing cards he designed for Loewe?
groundtruth = Picardo personalized the characters in the playing cards by portraying the King of Hearts as the Emperor Charlemagne, the King of Clubs as Goliath, the King of Diamonds as Julius Caesar, and the King of Spades as Alexander the Great.
predict_answer = 1951 Pic was commissioned by the Spanish fashion brand Loewe to design a deck of baraja (playing cards) for the company's "Exquisit" line of luxury products.The rules of Spain at that time required that the manufacture of playing cards be restricted to a small number of printers, none of whom were available to carry out the work, so Picardo — as a non-printer — could not produce the cards himself. He therefore collaborated with the Spanish professional card printer Fernando Paredes Viñas, who had his own patented machine for printing playing cards.In designing the cards, Picardo researched their history and symbolism and decided that they would be styled as an historical Andalucían deck, specifically as if they were from the era of the last Moorish rulers of Granada in the 16th century. The cards are in a pack, each measuring 8.5 by 5.4 centimetres.Picardo's design of the cards is highly elaborate and the decoration, through the borders, corners and backs, causing the whole card to be a complex pattern. The numbers and symbols are all formed in relief by embossing. The background colour of the cards is dark brown, representative of the land; the hearts, clubs and spades are coloured in bright red, blue and green respectively, while the diamonds are coloured gold. On the back of the cards Picardo featured his logo: name "J.L. Picardo" in stylised letters.At one end of each card is the name of the card in Spanish: for instance, at the top of the King of Hearts "Re deor." Below the name is the illustration of the character: for instance, for the King of Hearts a noble mounted on a horse, both in action. Below that is the coat of arms of the region or city which the card represents. On the left side of the card is the suit symbol in large, followed by the number of the card repeated in numerals and in words in Spanish. On the right side of the card is the artist's signature "J.L. Picardo".Below each illustration is placed a of verses in a single line, some describing the character, others making a general observation. For example, below the King of Hearts: "El re magnífico," (The king is magnificent), while under the Jack of Clubs: "El de la fortuna" (The luckiest).On the Master card, Picardo has placed the title "Baraja dea dees" (Game of cards by Picardo) in his characteristic style. Below that he has: "Este juego fue creado el año 1951." (This game was created in 1951). In the lower part he has described the stage of perfection: "perfección en su historia." (in its history).The Loewe/ardo baraja was produced in 1952 and the first edition, signed and numbered, was made up of 00 decks. It was published without announcement or publicity and within a year the entire first edition was sold.Pardo invited to return to his Baraja Andaluza to make improvements, and in 1966 he completed a second version which was a Parador de Guajara, a new public similar to those he had restored in the 1930s and 1940s. This set the standard for all future productions of the cards.. A third improved version was produced in 1975 which eliminated the previous defects in the display of the numbers on the cards being partly hidden by the shadow of the box. This version a best seller in Spain and abroad its elegant pastiche style. One American collector enthused about the cards: "I love these cards! They are beautiful, so historical and so ... it's almost impossible to describe." Others were not so convinced. British collector maintained years later that when the Andalucían deck was introduced "it was not well received, probably because it was a master piece."In 1980 Picardo was invited to the National Museum of Fine Arts in Madrid to judge competition for new Parador room designs. He declined, saying that he was busy with other projects. He suggested two young architects, Carlos Fernández-Cuenca Gómez and Mariano García-Ochoa Ibáñez, who had recently worked with him on the restoration of the Castillo de San Felipe in Puerto de la Cruz and who, like him, were members of the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando. They went on to win the contract to design a new wing for the Parador at Arcos de la Frontera in province of Cádiz, based on Picardo's earlier work there in 1937. Picardo was also asked to review their plans, which he did with enthusiasm.Despite his busy schedule, Picardo continued to work on Parador projects into the 1970s, though they were mostly minor commissions.

At one end of the ground floor was the hall and at the other end the dining room, with the bar and cafetería in between. In the interior decoration he copied many of the features, both large and small, he had used in the earlier Paradores, including the starry ceiling in the dining room. He also used his typical stone chimneys on the southern façade facing the room. On the inner face of the original west wall of the castle which enclosed the courtyard, Picardo installed a porticoed gallery on the ground floor, above it a gallery with balconied windows.In the decoration he copied many of the features he had used in the earlier Paradores, including the starry ceiling in the dining room. He also his typical stone chimneys on the southern façade facing the room. In the decoration of the Parador Picardo determined that the ground floor would be medieval in design in keeping with the original military use of the castle, and upper floors would be more palatial in decor. He designed much of the joinery, the beds, the tables, the chairs and, in particular, the light fittings, making use of the emblem of the Order of Calatrava as a decorative motif. He also used his typical ceramic tiles throughout the building, both for decoration and for explanatory texts.Picardo planned 18 guest rooms, but initially only 9 were built, some in the building facing the village, and the rest fronting the cliff view. latter benefitted from same design of open wooden galleries Picardo had utilised at Jaén and Guernica. The Parador opened to the public on 18 May 1968.Further guest rooms were built in 1972, using the same design, which brought the total to 18. In 1990 an expansion added a new wing by the architect Carlos Fernández-Cuenca Gómez which changed the character of the Parador. British travel writer, Peter, visited the Parador in 1972 and described it as "one of the best of the Paradores, its dramatic setting and unusual." Others have not been so convinced. British travel journalist wrote years later that the Parador was "magnificent externally, pitifully inside, the history having been destroyed by its conversion into a Parador."Another British writer, John, maintained years later that Guernica was "a parador with an attractive exterior, but bland and uninteresting inside." He went on: "Perhaps the worst feature is the modern extension which seems to have no regard for the original building." Parador de Carmona: Alcazar del Rey Don Pedro. In 1966 Picardo began the renovation of the Palacio del Rey Don Pedro (also known as the Alcázar de Arriba y Alcázar de Arriba y Alcázar de los Arqueros) in the small, historic Andalucían town of Carmona 37 kilometres east of Sevilla. The palace-fortress is the oldest extant in Seville. Most of its was built in the 13th century on pre-existing Arab and in Mudéjar style. By the time Picardo came to the palace it had been completely abandoned. groundtruth = He placed the reception area to the left and the bar and cafetería to the right.
predict_answer = 1965 he designed his first building, the Parador de Cáceres in the province of the same name in Extremadura. The castle had been allowed to fall into disrepair and parts had been demolished, but in 1925 it was declared a National Monument. Picardo began work on the Parador in early 1963 and his draft plans were ready by the late summer of that year. The building was situated on top of the hill overlooking the city and its purpose was as a hotel rather than as a Parador, which required conversion into a hotel).In his plans Picardo set the main structure of the building, a typical Hispanic-Arabic layout with two central patios, one of which would be the centre of the public area, and the other the centre of the service department. The layout would effectively reproduce that of the original fortress. He planned a first floor built of brick and an upper floor of stone, sloping roof, and would allow for 23 guest rooms.The first stage was building a new south wall of the building, which had been completely destroyed, in position that would allow for the hotel's required number of guest rooms. Picardo wanted a large window in this new wall, but by the height of the cliff the ground around the building there would not be enough headroom for windows of the size he wanted. His solution was to build a mezzanine level within the building, so that from that level above the main floor there would be sufficient height for the windows. The main floor would be flush with the parapet at the top of the wall and from that level Picardo could arrange the hotel's lounge, dining room and other public areas, while the mezzanine floor would have guest rooms looking out onto the balcony area below them.The main structure was Picardo's favoured style, a Hispanic-Arabic design with much use of arches and vaults, and a long corridor leading to the rooms around the patio, which he decorated with his typical ceramic tiles within his own mural images.In his second phase in 1972 Picardo added a further identical wing on the east side of the building, increasing the number of guest rooms to 41. He also built a large hall on the north side of the building, allowing for car parking beneath it. Through all his work at Cáceres Picardo maintained the mood of the original medieval fortress. Externally most of the walls were in naked stone and the roofs were clay tiling. Internally, he installed heavy wooden furniture, made much use of tile and stone and left the exposed wood of the beams and the inflooring. The dominant colours were deep ochre and dark brown.. To the left and right of the main entrance Picardo placed two towers, which set the standard for most of his later work for Paradores, particularly the larger ones. They provided for guest rooms within them, and for the hotel's opening hours. On the exterior of the towers Picardo featured relief sculptures and intricate ironwork and canopies. Above the main entrance he placed the coat of arms of Cáceres.The Parador opened to guests on 18 July 1966.In the late 1960s and early 1970s excessive rain caused a number of landslips in the unstable ground around the Parador and Picardo was regularly called in to strengthen the building.. Picardo returned to the project in 1972 to build a further extension duplicating the earlier east wing, so that the building became symmetrical. He was hampered by the layout of the available land, and by limitations in the height to which he could build, so the extension had to be built as a mirror image of the first wing, with the same layout and dimensions Despite the difficulties, Picardo completed the work in 1978, increased the number of guest rooms to 41. He was unable to accommodate more guests because of the of the land available.The Parador was inaugurated in 1978.Picardo also designed the building's interior, producing furniture, flooring, doors, windows, light fittings, mirrors, heraldic displays, seigneurial crests, explanatory mosaics and so on to continue emphasising the building's medieval ambience. He also used decorative plasterwork, tile and ironwork and stone throughout the building. His attention to detail even extended to the design of hinges and handles for doors, and for the heads of nails used in the door faces. He also used his typical ceramic throughout the building, both for decoration and for explanatory texts.Picardo built 23 single guest rooms, 18 double rooms, 5 suites, making a total guest complement of 6. Most of the rooms were on the floor, with some below the Parador's access level. One suite was located the tower, with others on the inner face of the tower facing the patio.
